findings.text: A file space mapping record carries a device identifier in fmr_device and mapping flags in fmr_flags followed by a device byte offset in fmr_physical and an owner identifier in fmr_owner and a file byte offset in fmr_offset and a byte length in fmr_length plus three reserved words in fmr_reserved that must stay zero. The first two fields are narrow and the remaining offsets and counts are wide.

A mapping query header carries input control flags in fmh_iflags and output flags in fmh_oflags and a total slot count in fmh_count including search keys and a filled output count in fmh_entries plus six wide reserved words that must stay zero and two key records in fmh_keys for low and high search bounds with a trailing flexible array fmh_recs for returned records.

The sizing helper reports the footprint of one header plus a caller supplied number of records. The advance helper copies the last returned record into the first search key so a later query resumes after prior output. Iteration therefore sizes a batch then queries then advances the low key from the final entry.
No input control bits are defined so FMH_IF_VALID has value zero. Output flag FMH_OF_DEV_T has value one and promises device identifiers are encoded as device numbers.

Record flags mark unwritten preallocation and attribute fork data and extent map data and shared blocks and special owner encoding and last record in the data set with numeric values one and two and four and eight and sixteen and thirty two respectively.

An owner packs a type in the upper half and a code in the lower half with accessors isolating each half. Free space and unknown owner and metadata use type zero with codes one through three. The mapping query uses FS_IOC_GETFSMAP with letter X and number fifty nine over the query header.

Enable arguments carry a version and a hash algorithm selector and a block size and a salt size plus a user pointer to salt and a signature size plus a user pointer to signature with reserved space. A measurement buffer carries an algorithm and a size field used both to supply capacity and return length with trailing digest bytes.
Supported verity digest selectors are one for SHA256 and two for SHA512.

The on disk descriptor requires version one and records Merkle hash algorithm and base two logarithm of block size and salt length and covered file size and a sixty four byte root hash and a thirty two byte salt area with one hundred forty four reserved zero bytes. Kernel builds expose a signature length and trailing signature bytes where user builds see reserved zero space.

A formatted digest starts with an eight character magic identifying FSVerity followed by algorithm and size fields with trailing digest bytes. A metadata read request carries a metadata type and an offset and a length and a destination pointer with a reserved word.

Metadata types are one for Merkle tree and two for descriptor and three for signature. Enable and measure and read metadata operations use letter f with numbers one hundred thirty three through one hundred thirty five over their respective argument structures.

Legacy crypto names alias version one policy and modern constants for descriptor size and a pad flag quartet with mask and a direct key flag and several cipher modes and descriptor prefix with prefix size and maximum key size. Valid old flags mask is seven and invalid mode is zero. Modes with values two and three for GCM and CBC exist but are marked never used.
Both the mapping and verity user headers define a once only inclusion guard macro.

Delay calibration exposes a fine loops value and a preset loops value parsed by lpj_setup plus a per processor loops value defaulting to zero and weak hooks for reporting a known value and for completion notification.

The per processor calibration entry selects among already calibrated state and preset value and fine timer value and architecture known value and direct timer measurement and convergent loop measurement then records the result both per processor and globally with single shot reporting and a completion hook.

Calibration follows an ordered preference from cached per processor value to preset to fine to known to direct and finally converge. Direct failure falls through to convergence. Publishing is followed by one global report and the completion hook.

Direct calibration measures a platform timer across a tick span that is one when HZ is below one hundred and otherwise HZ divided by one hundred. It repeats up to five attempts and keeps samples whose rate bounds agree within about one eighth while discarding wrap and jittered samples then drops the outlying extreme until the range fits or fails.
When direct timer support is absent the direct routine reports failure immediately so the caller falls back to convergent measurement.

Convergent calibration first grows a delay across tick boundaries to bracket one tick then refines by halving the adjustment down to an eight bit precision limit. If every refinement step succeeded it restarts with a larger range because the start likely underestimated severely.

Early mount code exposes default mount flags and a saved textual root name buffer of sixty four bytes and a wait setting and the chosen root device number plus optional mount data and filesystem name list and boot delay values.

Init handlers readonly and readwrite and root_dev_setup and rootwait_setup and rootwait_timeout_setup and root_data_setup and fs_names_setup and root_delay_setup validate empty or numeric input and update the corresponding mount state while rejecting malformed values without aborting boot.

A numeric root wait timeout is read as seconds and converted to milliseconds with overflow detection. Invalid or excessive input warns and falls back to indefinite wait represented by negative one. Bare root wait also selects indefinite wait.

A comma separated filesystem list is split in place into a counted sequence. A single mount attempt copies caller options into a full page and mounts at the fixed early root path and switches the current directory there and records the mounted superblock device while announcing name and read only state.

Generic root mounting enumerates either the requested filesystem list or all block filesystems. It tolerates access and argument failures by flushing pending releases and continuing. After exhausting writable attempts it retries once forced read only and otherwise lists partitions and filesystems before halting.

Network roots for types nfs and cifs each retry up to five times with a sleep starting at five seconds and doubling to a thirty second cap. Missing server data or exhausted attempts ends with an error message. Builds without support provide an empty operation.

Nodev mounting only tries filesystems declaring no device requirement and stops at first success. Block mounting creates a well known device node path slash dev slash root before delegating to generic logic. Device creation removes any prior node then creates a block node with a restrictive mode. An empty build provides no block operation.

Top level root mounting dispatches on the root device kind toward NFS and CIFS and generic handling. When the device number is zero and both a name and a filesystem list are present it tries nodev mounting with fall through to block on failure and otherwise uses block mounting.
The early boot entries mount_root and mount_root_generic are the externally reachable roots for selecting and instantiating the initial filesystem.
Deferred release flushing during early mount runs both delayed cleanup and pending task work.
Initial mount flags request read only silent mounting. The read only and read write handlers only accept empty values and respectively set or clear the read only flag.

Boot halts when the filesystem name buffer cannot be allocated and when the requested block target cannot be opened or no candidate filesystem succeeds. Direct delay estimation can fail after repeated jitter and then falls back to convergence. Malformed timeouts only warn and use indefinite wait.
